query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an α + β dual-phase alloy with low hardness and poor friction and wear properties under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Earlier studies explored redesigning the bulk alloy, which risks compromising its original advantages, and several surface-modification approaches. Traditional thermal spraying and thermal plating produced weak coatings with poor substrate bonding; composite coatings suffered from uneven constituent dispersion and weak interfaces; and laser cladding could generate intermetallic compounds, high residual stresses, cracks, and crazing. Prior refractory high-entropy-alloy studies reported improved hardness and wear resistance, but the broader requirements of compositional homogeneity, strong bonding, mechanical stability, and preservation of TC4’s beneficial properties remain. Formulate one neutral, testable hypothesis for an intervention that could satisfy these requirements. Specify the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Friction stir processing (FSP) of TC4 using a refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) filler will produce an in-situ, nano-dispersed HEA reinforcement in the surface region that significantly increases the surface hardness and wear resistance relative to untreated TC4, without compromising its bulk properties.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) dual-phase alloy with relatively low hardness and poor friction/wear performance under high-contact-stress conditions.
generation.intervention: Perform friction stir processing on the TC4 surface while introducing a refractory HEA filler material.
generation.conditions: Process the TC4 substrate under FSP conditions (below melting temperature, with controlled tool rotational and traverse speeds) such that the HEA filler is mixed into the top layer, achieving a uniform nano-dispersed distribution. Testing to be conducted under wear conditions similar to extreme service/high-contact-stress environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formation of fine, nano-dispersed HEA precipitates uniformly embedded within a refined grain structure in the TC4 surface layer.
generation.mechanism: During friction stir processing, the intense plastic deformation and frictional heat enable dynamic recrystallization of TC4 and simultaneous mixing with the added refractory HEA. The HEA forms nano-precipitates that enhance dispersion strengthening, while also refining the grain structure. This dual effect is expected to hinder dislocation motion and increase load-bearing capability, thereby improving surface hardness and wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated TC4 surface will exhibit a notable increase in hardness and a lower wear rate when tested under typical high-contact-stress conditions compared to untreated TC4.
generation.baseline: Untreated TC4 alloy exhibiting lower hardness and higher wear rate under similar testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only when processing parameters (temperature, tool speed, and HEA filler composition) are optimized to promote homogeneous dispersion and nano-scale precipitation. Extreme variations outside these parameters (e.g., excessive heat leading to intermetallic formation or cracking) may negate the beneficial effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the hardness increase and wear rate reduction is uncertain, and there is potential for unintended microstructural changes that could affect ductility or bonding at the interface if processing parameters are not strictly controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of TC4 samples: one set to be processed by FSP with the refractory HEA filler and a control set subjected to the same FSP conditions without the HEA filler. Ensure identical processing parameters (tool rotation, traverse speed, and applied load). After processing, perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, TEM) to confirm the presence and uniformity of nano-dispersed HEA precipitates, and conduct standardized microhardness and wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disk tests) on the treated surfaces.
measurements: Surface microhardness profile across the processed zone
Wear rate and coefficient of friction under controlled load and sliding distance
Microstructural characterization (grain size, HEA distribution, precipitate size)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP with HEA filler does not produce a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least 20% increase in hardness and a corresponding reduction in wear rate) relative to both untreated TC4 and the FSP-only control, or if the treated surfaces show poor bonding or detrimental microstructural defects, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Dispersion strengthening is a strengthening mechanism by which a large number of other external phases are added to the high-entropy alloy. As a result, the content of the phase in the high-entropy alloy far exceeds its solubility, thus dispersing the structure of other phases. TiC existed in the form of large-sized agglomerated particles in the coating, which bore the main load. This method belonged to load strengthening. Because the coefficient of thermal expansion of the TiC and HEA did not match, the dislocation density of the coating would increase. This phenomenon improved the overall performance of the coating [,,]. Grain refinement is a common strengthening mechanism. It mainly affects the grain size of the original composition by adding particles. The TiC particles would preferentially form cores in the high-entropy alloy systems, consuming a large amount of grain boundary energy to hinder the grain growth []. Friction Stir technique is one of the surface composite fabrication methodologies in which the composite fabrication is made well below the melting temperature of constituent materials. It is derived from friction stir welding in which a non-consumable tool is plunged into the surface for joining. FSP is a thermomechanical process derived from friction stir welding in which plastic deformation can yield an ultrafine. FSP has gained attention from researchers and industry as it modifies the microstructure of the material, improving ductility without forfeiting strength. More importantly, FSP is also a more economical and dependable technique for surface composite fabrication. It is very clear from the graphs shown in Figs. 3, 4, 5 that the reinforced HEA particles offer great influence on wear-resistant capability of copper matrix. The capability to resist the wear when sliding over the counterpart was momentously improved when the HEA particles were added and it improved further for every addition of the HEA reinforcing medium. The wear rate considerably declines on adding 5% HEA reinforcement with copper due to load carrying capability and increase in hardness of the copper with HEA addition. It could be concluded that higher material hardness leads to raised wear resistance. Therefore, the copper's resistance to wear is enhanced as the amount of high-entropy alloy (HEA) added increases, as this leads to an increase in the hardness of the copper. Moreover, the hardness of the copper matrix is enhanced due to the formation of a fine-grain structure resulting from the intense stirring action of the Friction Stir Processing (FSP) tool during the creation of test composite material.
